(Carter Jr, et al., 2020) talks about self-regulated learning, which can be defined 
as a learning style where the student takes control over the learning process 
including task completion, self-assessment, and adjusting their schemas. One of 
the key aspects of self-regulated learning is that it aims to improves student 
motivation by allowing the student to monitor and set personal goals on their 
progress (Lung-Guang, 2019). Goal setting, self-evaluation and other 
metacognitive activities are associated with improved academic performance. 
One of the downsides with self-regulated learning is that it contradicts with 
cognitive-load theory, by introducing extraneous load on students enforcing 
them to do metacognitive activities which may lead to worse performance 
(Carter Jr, et al., 2020; Van Merriënboer & Sluijsmans, 2009).  
(Doo, et al., 2023) expresses concern with self-directed learning, claiming that 
students must be of an independent mindset to perform well. They also mention 
that culture differences may impact its effectiveness. 
A middle ground where the extraneous load of self-assessment could be 
automated away from the student, which could help reduce the stress and 
confusion, and may help alleviate the downsides. Taking away the ability for the 
student to choose what they do would defeat the point of a self-regulated 
learning environment, but the option to follow a strict path may also reduce 
extraneous load.
